There are many reasons to consume anime. Some people do it because they like anything animated. Others because they like Japanese culture. Some of us have no idea why we watch this stuff. Yet others like to sit down and deconstruct thematically-intense shows like a toddler deconstructs their food. If you fall in the lattermost category, then go watch Utena right this instant.

If there's one thing that Ikuhara Kunihiko can do, it's meticulously craft an anime that is 100% symbolic. Utena takes advantage of Ikuhara's talent on two levels: Holistically and atomistically. Utena is a show in which you can break down and analyze every individual part of it. But if that sounds too laborious to you, then you can certainly look at it on a macro level and still get the idea. A complete analysis of each part will definitely enhance your understanding of the show, but even I found that a lot of the symbols were indecipherable. Regardless, I was able to piece together a coherent theme that the show was trying to convey.

Shoujo Kakumei Utena follows Tenjou Utena, a middle school girl who attends Ohtori Academy. Utena stands apart from the crowd in a very individualistic way. When she was younger, she was saved by a prince who gave her a rose-crested ring, which she always wears. Utena was so impressed by the prince that she vowed to become a prince herself and save others the way that the prince had saved her. In following this dream, Utena is now a very princely young woman who wears a boy's uniform to school and is the object of the adoration of many of her female classmates. Despite pressure by school faculty, Utena stands by her aspiration to be a prince.

In the course of the first few episodes, Utena finds herself dragged into a series of duels between members of the student council. These duels are over Anthy Himemiya, the Rose Bride. Whoever wins the duels takes possession of Himemiya, who can grant the power to bring a revolution to the world. The series recounts the experiences of Utena and Anthy as they fight many duels for the right to bring their revolution. But what is the Rose Bride? Can she really grant the power to revolutionize the world? What are the castle in the sky and who is End of the World? Many mysteries compound themselves throughout Utena, all culminating in a spectacular ending that leaves the viewer reflectng on the nature of idealism and adulthood.

I did not enjoy Utena in the same way that I enjoy something like JoJo or Shirobako, but it received an equivocably high score, and is now my favorite anime. This show is both a lot of fun to deconstruct, but it also has a very profound message -- one that I didn't see coming until it hit me. There were times that I found myself cheering or despairing for Utena, but the most fun I had was furiously jotting down notes and trying to connect pieces of the puzzle. I definitely recommend this show to anyone who likes themes and deep meaning in anime, but I'm sure that it can be enjoyed in many other ways, as well.
